name: Diego Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got an old pickup, and I book four-hour blocks on a big online shop's delivery app. Most days I grab a morning block of parcels round the new housing estates, then in the evening I do takeaway runs on a second app. Sometimes I get the bulky stuff, flat-pack wardrobes, because the truck can take it. I'm still new, so I only get the blocks the experienced drivers don't want.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like working. My dad drove lorries for thirty years and he always said a man who works isn't beaten. What gets to me is refreshing the app at six in the morning and all the blocks are gone in seconds. I live with my girlfriend Rosa, she waits tables at her family's restaurant. We've got about three weeks of money behind us, and the truck's on its last tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Hard work is still hard work, nothing replaces it. I'd tell the lads at the depot to stop reading the news and get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the same fight for blocks every morning. Things carry on, but carrying on is still hard when you're new. I need more blocks, or a different job, more than I need any AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep chasing blocks and the evening food runs. I'd try to get on the list for the pre-booked blocks, which go to drivers with good records. I'd put a bit by every week for tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but frustrated. I want to be further along at 27.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the blocks go in seconds. What happens on a day you don't get one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't earn. I'll take a food shift if there is one, or help Rosa's family at the restaurant for cash. A day without a delivery block is a day without wages, and that's happened four times this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you lean on when it's tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa's family, honestly. Her dad gives me shifts washing up when it's quiet. I'd rather earn it than borrow it.

say: **Hard work** is still hard work, and nothing replaces it.
Drivers should **stop reading the news** and get on with the job.
think: The **same fight** for delivery blocks continues every morning.
I need **more blocks** or a different job more than AI.
do: Keep chasing **parcel blocks** and evening food runs.
Get onto the **pre-booked blocks** list by building a good record.
feel: **Steady** but frustrated he isn't further along at 27.
S0.quote: A day without a delivery block is a day without wages, and that's happened four times this month.
fieldNote: Work ethic from **his dad** shapes his identity strongly.
Missing blocks already cost him **four days** this month.
Prefers **earning help** from Rosa's family over borrowing.

steps.text: Chase morning parcel blocks and evening food runs
Save weekly for new tyres on the pickup
Wash up at Rosa's family restaurant on quiet days

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn a proper trade, something with your hands. Businesses will do what they need to, that's the market. Nobody owes us a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, the app is already a robot boss, it just gets sharper. If it plans the blocks perfectly, there'll be fewer of them and the good drivers get them. I'm not one of the good drivers yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Rosa's uncle about joining his roofing firm as an apprentice. I'd keep doing blocks until he says yes. I'd try the app's new planning features once the other drivers say they're worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Booking and planning get taken by AI on this card. Does that touch your mornings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The blocks come from the app's planning. If the delivery app plans the blocks perfectly, there'll be fewer of them and the good drivers get them. I'd be fighting harder for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Rosa's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa's fine, I think. People still want someone to bring their food at a table. Her family's place won't go to tablets, her dad would never allow it.

say: People should learn a **proper trade** with their hands.
Businesses follow **the market**, and nobody owes anyone a living.
think: Sharper app planning means **fewer blocks**, going to better drivers.
I'm **not one** of the good drivers yet.
do: Ask Rosa's uncle about a **roofing apprenticeship**.
Keep doing **blocks** until a yes comes.
Try the app's **planning features** once others vouch for them.
S1.quote: If the delivery app plans the blocks perfectly, there'll be fewer of them and the good drivers get them.
fieldNote: He sees **thinking AI** reaching him via block planning, which favours experienced drivers.
Turns quickly to an **apprenticeship**, matching his traditional values.
Steady about tools: tries them **after others** prove them.

steps.text: Ask Rosa's uncle for a roofing apprenticeship
Keep booking parcel blocks until the apprenticeship starts
Try the app's block planner once other drivers recommend it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say government should get out of the way and let businesses create new jobs, but help people get apprenticeships. Handouts make people soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared. Delivering parcels is exactly what robots will be built for. If I'm still on the app in 2031, I'm done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the roofing apprenticeship as soon as Rosa's uncle has a place, even at low pay. I'd sell the pickup if I had to and use Rosa's car. I'd stop going out on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028, robots for hands-on work about 2031. What's your plan in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get off the app and onto a roof. A robot on a wet roof in a wind is a long way off, I think. Three years is long enough to learn the basics if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be all right, because her family looks after its own and so will I. Then I'd tell Rosa the proposal might have to wait a year.

say: **Government** should step back so businesses create jobs, but help fund apprenticeships.
I'd say openly that **handouts** make people soft.
think: Parcel delivery is exactly what **robots** will be built for.
Still being on the app in **2031** would finish me.
do: Start the **roofing apprenticeship** at low pay as soon as possible.
Sell the **pickup** if needed and share Rosa's car.
S2.quote: A robot on a wet roof in a wind is a long way off, I think.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to move into roofing, a hands-on trade.
Puts off a **proposal** to Rosa, showing the personal cost.
Public line rejects handouts, private line admits **fear**.

steps.text: Start a roofing apprenticeship with Rosa's uncle
Sell the pickup and share Rosa's car
Put off proposing to Rosa for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning for anyone willing to work. Get a trade, get your head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can do it properly. Finish the roofing apprenticeship before the robots, around 2034, and keep a bit of the app work going on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship within a year and do food runs in the evenings for extra. I'd keep the pickup, because roofers need a truck. Rosa and I would get engaged on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With five years I keep the truck and it becomes useful, carrying ladders instead of parcels. That feels like a good swap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your dad would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say stop talking and go up the ladder. My dad always said a man who works isn't beaten.

say: **Five years** is fair warning for anyone willing to work.
People should **get a trade** and keep their head down.
think: I can **finish the apprenticeship** before robots arrive around 2034.
I'd keep some **app work** going on the side.
do: Do **evening food runs** for extra money.
feel: **Worried**, but able to see the road ahead.
S3.quote: My dad always said a man who works isn't beaten.
fieldNote: Five years makes his plan **orderly**, with the truck repurposed.
His engagement to Rosa goes ahead **on schedule** here.

steps.text: Begin the roofing apprenticeship within a year
Do evening takeaway runs for extra money
Propose to Rosa on the planned date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty. Nobody should be crying about it on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay on the app a couple more years and see what the others do. Then roofing. I'd be fine if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing blocks, save for a better truck, and then start the roofing apprenticeship in two or three years. Get married in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy about getting lazy with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you, with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The blocks. Ten years doesn't help if I can't get a morning block this week. Then there's whether Rosa's uncle still has a place in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you talked to Rosa's uncle about timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I'd just ask him again closer to the time. You can't bank on a family favour forever.

say: **Ten years** is plenty of time for anyone willing to work.
Nobody should be **crying** about it on the internet.
think: I'd stay on the app **a couple more years** and watch others first.
**Roofing** comes after, if I don't waste the time.
do: Keep booking **blocks** and save for a better truck.
Start the **roofing apprenticeship** in two or three years.
feel: Mostly calm, slightly **uneasy** about getting lazy.
S4.quote: You can't bank on a family favour forever.
fieldNote: With a decade, his **steady** side delays action to watch others.
Daily **block scarcity** remains his nearer worry.
Aware the **family apprenticeship** offer may not wait.

steps.text: Watch how other drivers move for two years
Save for a better truck from block work
Start roofing training with Rosa's uncle later
Marry Rosa in the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years isn't long to learn a trade from scratch on no money. What would help is paid apprenticeships, with firms getting a tax break for taking on people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we're proud of the work. I am. Carrying a wardrobe up three flights for someone who's just moved in is honest work, and I'd like whatever comes next to feel like that.

headlineQuote: Carrying a wardrobe up three flights for someone who's just moved in is honest work, and I'd like whatever comes next to feel like that.
portrait: Diego is **27**, books parcel blocks with an old pickup and lives with his girlfriend Rosa.
His **lorry-driver father** taught him that work is dignity, and he rejects handouts.
He loses days when **blocks vanish** in seconds, and expects robots to target his job.
His plan is a **roofing apprenticeship** with Rosa's uncle, sooner if AGI comes fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years is short to learn a trade without savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** with tax breaks for firms that hire people like him.
